articles.text: Residents near Triangle Park meet with city about memorial On Saturday, December 2, at Triangle Park on Wildwood and Magnolia Avenues, the city of Piedmont hosted an event to describe plans for the Sidney & Irene Dearing Memorial. It will memorialize Piedmont’s first black homeowners who were driven out of town approximately 100 years ago. Invitations went out to 200 residents living nearby. The event was intended to let community members voice their input on the memorial’s development, including what they like about the park, how they use the space, and how the memorial could be best integrated into the park. The event was organized by City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, and Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. Bayon Moore provided the project’s history, followed by an hour-long session where city officials heard neighbors’ questions, comments, and concerns about the space. “We looked to learn more about how residents use the park today and asked them to share any neighborhood-specific needs we should consider while developing design concepts,” she said. “Many of the neighbors in the immediate vicinity really cherish the existing space,” said Gonzales. “Children in the community use it frequently, and it is a lovely, wooded area that feels almost secluded. And everyone seems to appreciate the existing redwood trees that are there”. The Sidney and Irene Dearing memorial is the city’s response to a dark chapter in Piedmont’s history. Sidney and Irene Dearing purchased a home in 1924 and were Piedmont’s first black homeowners. A mob of white residents, abetted by the city council and police, forced the couple to sell their house and move. A memorial for Sidney & Irene Dearing was officially announced by the city on October 24, 2023. Hood Design Studio was chosen to create a memorial. The future site of the Sidney & Irene Dearing Memorial, beloved by the community for its seclusion and proximity to nature.

articles.text: The following letter was sent to Kevin Jackson, City Planner for the City of Piedmont. Dear Mr. Jackson: I attended the November 30 community workshop about the proposed Moraga Canyon housing project. You and I spoke about several issues, and you welcomed me to send you follow-up observations. I am concerned about the project’s isolation, the low-income residents’ separation, and the willingness of the project’s managers to incorporate community feedback into the plans. No opportunity was given for workshop attendees to question the project planners as a group. General questions about the overall nature of the project would not be answered by staff personnel who were designated to discuss specific options at individual poster-board stations. This gave me and several other people the feeling that the City isn’t really interested in hearing and addressing our concerns. I am concerned about the isolation of the 132 new units planned for the Moraga area. There is no “urban fabric” connecting that location with the rest of Piedmont, except for the heavily-trafficked Moraga Ave. Walkers or bike riders would not see other Piedmont houses for over a quarter mile. Isolation may be a more severe problem for residents of the 60 subsidized units who may not have cars available for both going to work and for shopping or going to school. This problem could be mitigated if the City were to operate a shuttle bus, similar to the shuttles that Emeryville operates to and from BART. The City could operate the shuttle for the first five years, and then evaluate whether the amount of ridership justifies continuing. A more serious problem is the planned separation of the below-market units from the market-rate units. This is a terrible idea that will have dangerous consequences. It would create a low-income “ghetto” in the midst of high-income housing. While you agreed that integration was a good idea, Mr. Jackson, you contended that separation was necessary because the subsidized housing had to be built as a separate project. This was not my experience when I developed housing for low and moderate income people, financed by both Federal and State programs ago. Section 8 below-market rental housing units were part of a larger market-rate project financed through HUD (the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development). There was no physical difference between the rental units. Some of the 132 units could be sold to individuals (72 at market rate, 60 at below-market rate), with unsold units being sold to a non-profit agency which would rent the market-rate units and the subsidized units together, with no physical distinction among the units. They would be seamlessly included within the 132-unit project. No ghetto. No separation. There are many different ways to finance such mixed-income projects – direct subsidies, tax credits, a combination of county, State and Federal funding, perhaps even some philanthropy. I hope the planning consultants and the City Council act on these concerns and respond to community residents’ feedback. –Bruce Joffe Piedmont resident 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Matt Simons, Lead reporter Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Jay Russell SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Jeremy Randolph provides details on newly planned EV Hub Last month, the Shell station at the corner of Wildwood and Grand Avenues was sold back to the Shell corporation after nearly 17 years of private operation and ownership by Jeff Hansen under the name Piedmont Auto Care. On Thursday, November 16, Shell announced they would replace the existing structure with a new, 14-bay electric vehicle (EV) charging hub under the Shell Recharge brand. An open house for neighbors was held at Kehilla Community Synagogue on Tuesday, November 28, where Shell representatives answered residents’ questions about the new EV Hub. Until recently, the project has lacked a central figure that community members could recognize and direct their questions toward. Questions may now be directed to Jeremy Randolph, the new program manager of the Shell Recharge EV Hub. This week, the company announced that Randolph would be the “focal contact” for the company, “overseeing all activities regarding this project.” Originally from Miami, Florida, Randolph has lived in Oakland since 2021. He attended college at Florida State University where he studied Mechanical Engineering. In the past, he has worked on projects in both charging infrastructure and electric vehicle design. He became involved with Shell in 2022 and has been with the company for a little over a year. He currently lives in downtown Oakland, only 10 minutes away from the site of the new Shell Recharge Hub. Randolph said that Shell chose Piedmont as the EV Hub’s new location based on several criteria, including “a lack of nearby charging facilities – specifically, fast chargers.” If approved by the City of Piedmont, Randolph believes the new Shell Recharge hub will help address this need and allow drivers to refuel between trips. Pricing at the new station will be on a pay-as-you-go basis. Just as at home, charging prices will vary based on the time of day. Drivers will be able to find the real-time cost of their charge via the Shell app. The app will also allow drivers to locate the nearest charger, check the station’s charging status and make payments. In contrast with the previous gas station, Randolph confirmed there will be no employees on-site regularly at the new EV Staff Photo Jeremy Randolph answers questions from community members at Shell’s open house on Tuesday, November 28.

articles.text: Donation bins will remain out until December 23 The Piedmont Fire Department has received an abundance of donations for the annual Toys for Tots drive. The Piedmont Fire Department is currently accepting donations for the annual Toys for Tots drive through December 23. Piedmont residents are encouraged to donate new unwrapped toys and place them in donation bins at the Piedmont Fire Station, 120 Vista Avenue. “Our annual toy drive is one of the favorite times of the year for Piedmont’s firefighters. We enjoy every time a community member brings in donations of new toys,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “Working with Toys for Tots and Three Wise Men toy giveaway ensures the community’s generosity reaches as many children as possible.” Donated toys will be distributed to families in Oakland and Alameda County, and any toys donated before December 8 will be distributed through the US Marine Corps Reserve’s Toys for Tots Foundation. Toys donated after December 8 will be distributed at the annual Three Wise Men toy giveaway in Oakland’s Fruitvale neighborhood. Bins will remain at City Hall for donations through December 23. articles.text: The City of Piedmont announced on Tuesday, December 12 the launch of a new online permitting system for Planning, Building, and Public Works permits. The new system, called “eTRAKiT,” is designed to serve as a “one-stop shop” for all permit-related activities. It will allow community members to apply for and check the status of their applications in real-time. As a result, the City will no longer accept paper or email applications for most planning, building, and public works permit types. These applications now must be handled through eTRAKiT. City officials hope that these changes will make the overall permit process simpler, increase accountability in city staff, and ultimately decrease wait times for residents seeking permits. According to Paki Muthig, Building Official with the Planning & Building Department, this update has been a long time coming. Piedmont is facing a mandate from the State of California to introduce these changes by January 2024, but a public portal for city permits has been planned since Muthig was hired by the City in 2018. Muthig was excited about the efficiency the new process promises. “Now, as a user, you will be able to look at the status of your permit at any time. You don’t have to call and say, ‘Hey, where’s my permit?’ You’ll know. And it won’t just sit on someone’s desk for 16 weeks,” said Muthig. Muthig insisted that the adoption of eTRAKiT would not affect the in-person staffing of his department and that eTRAKiT is not intended to replace the department’s workers. The Planning & Building Department will still assist with permitting through eTRAKiT on the phone and in-person at one of their two kiosk stations, now present at City Hall. The average time to process building permits in Piedmont is currently 2-4 weeks for small projects and 5-8 weeks for permits for larger jobs. During the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, applicants faced wait times nearing 16 weeks because of backed-up department workloads. With their new system, the city hopes to decrease these times. The eTRAKiT system is used by 60 cities and counties in California. For questions about eTRAKiT, please call (510) 420-3050 or email buildingpermits@piedmont.ca.gov. Staff photo Piedmont Building Official Paki Muthig shows off the new eTRAKiT system at a kiosk in City Hall. Members of the public are invited to use these stations to apply for permits.

articles.text: Negotiations over the contracts of Piedmont teachers will take a new step on Thursday, December 14, when both sides will meet the assigned Mediator Ken Glenn at 1:30 p.m. Once mediation has begun the two sides will be prohibited from talking about points of discussion. Glenn was appointed by the Public Employment Relations Board last month and will soon be called on to end the impasse between teachers and school district. The Association of Piedmont Teachers union (APT) will retain the same negotiation team consisting of APT President Elise Marks, Mercedes Foster, Ben Spencer, Craig Best, and Katie Terhar along with California Teachers Association Representative Gray Harris. The district’s current offer allots for 2% raises for this school year, 4% next year and 3% the year after that. APT is asking for 8.22% this year which is the Cost of Living Adjustment amount determined by inflation in the state. “No matter how tight the budget is, more money must somehow be found.” said Marks to the Post. “Educators are stretched too tight financially as it is, and cannot sacrifice even more to balance the district budget.” Thursday’s mediation will signal a pause on updates given to the public, and even to members of the teachers union not on the negotiating team. Before the mandated public silence around negotiations APT members will rally for support outside City Hall at 5:30 p.m. on Wednesday, December 13. Marks and APT will make a brief statement before the closed session. They have called on members of the community to participate in the open session of the school board which starts at 7:00 p.m. tonight.

articles.text: Kids who stutter have a lot to say, and friends can show them how in Stuttering: For Kids By Kids, a DVD in English and Spanish, starring kids who stutter. It is available at most public libraries and through inter-library loans. Many children who stutter have never met others who struggle with the same disability. In this DVD from the Stuttering Foundation, they meet kids who recount how they handle challenges such as teasing, speaking out in class, and teaching others about stuttering. Swish, a lively and engaging animated basketball character designed by students at Purdue University, narrates the DVD. The children, who range in age from first grade to high school, offer frank and sometimes differing views of stuttering. For example, Matthew, age 10, says “It’s no big deal,” but Kate, age 9, worries about talking, what is going to happen next and whether or not she’ll stutter. Arianne, age 14, says, “The hardest part about stuttering is to get through it and to stay in there when you’re stuck.” Umang, age 12, agrees: “Sometimes it gets kind of annoying when you want to say something and you can’t. I also get worried what other people might think if I stutter and wonder if I’ll be able to get out of my blocks.” “All those interested in helping kids learn more about stuttering will want to see this tape,” said speech-language pathologist Bill Murphy of Purdue University. “The children featured are a perfect example of how to openly and honestly handle stuttering.” “This is an important tool for families and teachers of kids who stutter,” added Jane Fraser, president of the nonprofit Stuttering Foundation. Other professionals and specialists in stuttering in this production include Kristin Chmela of Northwestern University, Joe Donaher of Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, Lisa Scott of Florida State University, and Lee Caggiano of Friends. Since 1947, the nonprofit Stuttering Foundation has provided free materials to public libraries nationwide. A library that will shelve them can download a request form at stutteringhelp.org/libraries-information or email info@stutteringhelp.org.

articles.text: As we enter the heart of the giving season, our community faces a critical challenge: securing the remaining funds for the Piedmont School Giving Campaign. With just weeks to go, we stand $800,000 short of our ambitious yet essential $3.5 million goal. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team returned to the pitch last week with two victories to open its 2023 season. They traveled to Hayward for a 2-1 victory on Wednesday, December 6, and also defeated Tennyson in Hayward 2-0 two days later. Both teams are non-league opponents in the Shoreline Division; Piedmont plays in the upper Foothill Division. Piedmont continued its usual stifling system under coach Todd Sullivan, where the Highlanders press high to quickly regain possession and force teams to beat them with long balls in counterattack situations. “We’ve worked in practice on our high press, in particular on goal kicks. I was pleased the way we executed. We had to play a wet and slick field, so it was a case of playing more risk averse soccer,” said Sullivan. Hayward’s lone goal came on a penalty kick in the final minute of the game. Other than that, the Farmers struggled to create opportunities with just one threatening look on a counterattack in the 10th minute. Bosco Lorin and Aiden Woolwine scored goals against Hayward, and the Highlander offense unleashed 13 shot attempts with six on target, rarely allowing Hayward out of its own half. Bernales and Woolwine scored one goal each in the 2-0 shutout of Tennyson. The two games marked the first varsity starts for wingers Lorin and Gianluca Bini, who link up well with Woolwine and Bernales. The two are tall, rangy forwards who allow Piedmont to play vertically. “I thought we played with good energy,” said Bernales. “Eight of our players are new to varsity, but most of us have been playing together since we were about seven years old. articles.text: Soccer team wins 6-1 vs. Skyline, 5-0 over Tennyson Staff Photos Hannah Sullivan scored four goals and one assist against Tennyson. She also scored against Skyline. Two games with a +11 goal differential is an impressive way to start your soccer season. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team recently shut out Tennyson 5-0 on Thursday, December 7 after opening the season with a 6-1 victory at Skyline in Oakland on Tuesday, December 5. “We have a lot of new players and I’m happy with how we’re playing,” said coach Dan Chubbock. “We’re linking up quite well. As the games get tougher, we’re going to have to improve and our defense is going to get tested more. But I’m happy with how it’s looking. Even though we lost a big group of seniors from last year, we’ve kept the same style of play.” Junior Hannah Sullivan was especially impressive with four goals and an assist in Piedmont’s 5-0 shutout of Tennyson. She also scored her first varsity goal against Skyline. “It’s all very new in these first few games, but I think we have great chemistry in the final third. It’s been really fun working together and improving that side of our game,” said Sullivan. Piedmont’s attack was dominant in both games, with frequently shots on goal, Against Tennyson, the Highlanders had 39 shot attempts with 21 on target. “We have a lot of good chemistry, especially in the midfield,” said midfielder Louisa Symkowick. “Juliana [Thornborrow] and I have played together for a long time, and Elsa [Wallway] is fitting in perfectly. The connections we make benefit in every aspect, not just building out from the back, but getting the ball to the front – like how Hannah got her goals.” 5-0 win over Tennyson It didn’t take long for Piedmont to get on the board. Sullivan scored in the second minute of action. From there, PHS recorded eight shot attempts before their next goal in the 16th when Sullivan cleaned up a shot on target from Juliana Thornborrow. The Highlanders went into halftime holding a 2-0 lead and recorded 12 shot attempts in the remaining time. In the second half, Sullivan required just seconds to land her third goal for a hat trick right out of the gate in the 41st minute. Lola Biehn then assisted Sullivan on her fourth goal two minutes later for a 4-0 lead. Sullivan assisted Biehn for the game’s final goal in the 63rd minute. PHS still pressed on for more goals and h ad nine more shots in the remaining 17 minutes of action. 6-1 over Skyline Piedmont opened its season with a convincing 6-1 win over Skyline. Ava Sauer scored first for Piedmont after cleaning up a blocked shot by Darcy McKee. Later in the first half, McKee jumped on a sloppy pass back to the center back, wheeling it into the penalty area for a goal. Thornborrow then scored the third after a receiving a throughball into the area by McKee. In the second half, Thornborrow made it 4-0 after receiving a pass from a corner kick. Thornborrow then assisted Sullivan for her first varsity goal, 5-0. After a Skyline goal, Ryo Woltag put them game away with a nice shot from a couple of feet above the penalty area. articles.text: Staff Photos Brit Burden was elected to the Chris Huber Classic All-Tournament team. Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team wrapped up a strong performance in the 9th annual Chris Huber Classic at Acalanes in Lafayette from Thursday through Saturday, December 7-9, winning two of its three games. They opened with a narrow 52-48 loss to Monte Vista, then defeated De Anza 62-37 and beating St. Joseph 58-49 on the final day. The loss to Monte Vista comes against a Division 1 North Coast Section team that is undefeated thus far at 7-0. The Mustangs went 19-10 last year and received the No. 4 seed in the Div. 1 NCS postseason playoffs. “It was a great game against Monte Vista and we almost pulled off the win,” said PHS coach Ben Spencer. Brit Burden was selected for the All-Tournament team, Dillon Casey received an Honorable Mention, and Thorin Holmes was awarded the Chris Huber Inspirational Award. 58-49 over St. Joseph Piedmont led 18-15 at the end of the first quarter and took a commanding 36-23 advantage through the second quarter. But in the third, St. Joe outscored Piedmont 17-9 to cut the Highlanders’ lead to 45-40. Piedmont’s defense rallied in the fourth quarter to limit the Pilots to nine points, while scoring 13 to win 58-49. In the fourth quarter, the Pilots hit a 3-pointer to cut Piedmont’s lead to 48-43, but Dillon Casey and Ravi Silverberg quickly responded with 3-pointers to put the Highlanders up 54-43. Final stats: Casey led the way with 19 points, Burden scored 17, Silverberg had 15 points, Declan Linnane had five. Thorin Holmes had eight rebounds. Dillon Casey scored 19 points against St. Joseph and had double-doubles against De Anza and Monte Vista.

We named him The Post’s 2023 Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year. So far this season, Harris has appeared in all seven games for 102 minutes, scoring 48 total points on 19 field goals (45 percent) and two 3-pointers, to go along with 17 rebounds, nine assists, and two steals. He finished his illustrious Piedmont High career as the school’s all-time leading scorer with 1,570 points after playing in just two full varsity seasons and an abbreviated 2021 season due to COVID-19. Harris was named the WACC’s Co-Player of the Year alongside Berkeley’s Samir O’Brien. The Highlanders went 19-10 with Harris carrying the load as the team’s leading scorer and rebounder. articles.text: Offering a snappy spin for the holiday season, San Francisco Playhouse is staging a new look at the Broadway hit Guys and Dolls with performances through Saturday, January 13. Helmed by San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English with music direction by Dave Dobrusky and choreography by Nicole Helfer, the new production reexamines the classic musical, bringing alive writer Damon Runyon’s gritty world of New York’s Lower East Side and Harlem during the 1930s. Filled to the brim with beloved Broadway standards including “Luck Be a Lady,” “Sit Down, You’re Rocking the Boat,” and “I’ve Never Been in Love Before,” the production premiered on Broadway in 1950, winning the Tony Award for Best Musical. It has since received five Broadway revivals and has been performed around the world. The Washington Post lauded “Frank Loesser’s priceless score” and called the show a “magnitude of delight.” In 2015, The New York Times said, “There are many students of the form who proclaim ‘Guys and Dolls’ the best musical comedy ever, and they may well be right.” Inspired by Runyon’s stories about post-Prohibition New York, Frank Loesser, Abe Burrows, and Jo Swerling’s beloved musical tale of gamblers, gangsters, and betting on love follows two unlikely pairs: a high-roller wooing a cautious missionary to win a bet, and a burlesque dancer whose slippery long-time fiancé won’t commit. An uplifting story of redemption perfect for the holiday season, the San Francisco Playhouse (450 Post Street) is performing matinee and evening performances through January 13. Tickets ($15-$125) and more details are available at sfplayhouse.org, or through the box office at 415-677-9596. articles.text: Photo by Stefan Cohen The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus will perform their Holiday Spectacular this Sunday December 17 at Zellerbach Hall. The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus will perform its annual Holiday Spectacular this Sunday, December 17 at Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. Audiences can watch as the 100-member-strong, critically acclaimed chorus performs beloved holiday classics like “Jingle Bells” and “I’ll Be Home for Christmas” alongside timely, funny sketches in an event that has become a much-anticipated highlight of their performance season. Now celebrating its 45th year, the Chorus sparked a nationwide LGBTQ+ choral movement after its first public performance at a vigil on the steps of San Francisco’s City Hall following the assassinations of Supervisor Harvey Milk and Mayor George Moscone in 1978. Since then, the chorus has received critical recognition, organized national tours, and released several albums of original music. The show will be performed without intermission and last approximately 90 minutes. Tickets may be purchased at calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in-person at the Zellerbach Hall box, open Tuesday – Friday from 12:00 – 5:30 p.m. and Saturday – Sunday, 1 p.m.–5 p.m. Tickets are halfprice for UC Berkeley Students. Additional information can be found online at www.calperformances.org/2023-24-season.

Directed by Frances McDormand in Nomadland Review by Chris Honoré If you love movies, if you find extraordinary their ability to tell stories that encompass a wide spectrum of the human condition, then Nomadland is a film not to be missed. It won two Academy Awards in 2021, for Best Picture and for Chloé Zhao as Best Director. The narrative focuses on Fern, a 61-year-old woman, a character inhabited flawlessly by the remarkable, endlessly courageous, Oscar-winning actor Francis McDormand (Fargo; Three Billboards Outside Ebbin, Missouri). The film opens with Fern preparing to leave Empire, Nevada. She has recently lost her husband, and now, after years working in a gypsum plant, she has lost her job when the factory closes its doors. So Fern begins packing up her aging van, and, having found no work in the area, decides to leave Empire for warmer climes in the Southwest. Nomadland soon reveals itself to be a quirky, quietly profound, and a deeply human road story. She gradually discovers that while she is decidedly alone, she is not isolated, and soon comes across people at rest stops, most her age or older, living by choice in similarly converted vans. They view themselves as nomads, befriend one another, barter, give advice and share lessons of the road. They drift, and all seem to agree it’s not the destination but the journey. When leaving a camp they simply wave and say, “See you down the road.” Absent a traditional plot, Nomadland is a collection of compelling, interesting encounters with fellow nomads who embrace the beautiful desert vistas and distant horizons. Fern stops at a camp, perhaps takes a job, shares roadie vignettes, gleans a road less traveled wisdom from old-timer Bob Wells (playing himself), or the stoic Swankie (also portraying herself). And then moves on. McDormand is so wonderfully talented, she seems to be one of the drifters the filmmakers happen to meet as they assemble nomads where they find them, all seemingly content to inhabit society’s remote fringe. Surprisingly there is not a moment of bitterness in Fern’s encounters. Instead, we see a kind of resilient optimism. As an aside, there are only two actors in Nomadland: McDormand and David Strathairn as Dave. While they consider a relationship, Fern is unable to commit to anything more than the road. Finally, this tapestry of drifters (“not homeless but houseless”), captured in this film, can easily be characterized as an ethnographic revelation of a people who are otherwise all but invisible. articles.text: Sunny Pawar and Abhishek Bharate in Lion The challenge inherent in reviewing a splendid film such as Lion is how to offer the reader a sense of the film and yet give nothing away. Perhaps the only aspects of the story that should be disclosed are those shown in the trailer, three minutes that give just enough information to frame what will be a life changing event in a small boy’s life. Saroo (newcomer Sunny Pawar in a spectacular performance) is 5-years-old. His mother is a laborer in a rock quarry in Khandwa, India. He and his older brother, Guddu (Abhishek Bharate), scramble each day to supplement the family’s small income, often stealing coal from passing trains. Poverty defines the family, but the boys are resilient and deeply close. One night, Guddu ventures out to find anything he can sell or trade and tells Saroo he must stay at home. Saroo begs to go along and finally Guddu relents. At a local train station, Saroo is sleepy, exhausted, and Guddu leaves him on a bench, telling him not to wait for him. Saroo promises and immediately falls asleep. When he wakes, some hours later, the station is empty and all is quiet. He calls out for Guddu but hears only silence. He wanders over to an empty train waiting trackside and makes the fateful decision to go on board. Finding a softer seat than the station bench, he again falls asleep. When he awakens it is daylight and the train is moving, the countryside flashing by. He runs up and down the vacant aisles, calling out for Guddu… for anyone. The train does not stop until it reaches a station in Kolkata (Calcutta) and massive numbers of people, waiting on the platform, begin to board. Saroo pushes his way off the train, looking around for anything familiar. What he is unaware of is that he is 1,000 miles away from home and at a complete loss as how to get back. He doesn’t know where back is. He is suddenly alone. Lost. Endless crowds of people move around him, ignoring him, like a small rock in a rushing stream. This long first act is gripping, breathtaking, filled with heartfelt tension. How will small Saroo ever survive on the urban streets where predatory adults victimize abandoned children? And so begins a brief act two, which leads into act three and we meet a grown Saroo (Dev Patel) whose life has been completely transformed. But for his older Saroo, what was once lost now must be found. Be prepared to be captured by this wonderful film. It will touch you as you absorb not only little Saroo’s circumstances, but as you later engage with him as a young man. Both Dev Patel and Nicole Kidman were nominated for Golden Globe Awards for their very fine performances in Lion. Lion. Directed by Garth Davis. Starring Dev Patel, Nicole Kidman, Rooney Mara. 2 hrs. articles.text: Holidays at Filoli Gardens is open through January 7. Visit Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside to see the 16-acre estate brightly illuminated for the holidays. The nonprofit historical landmark will be celebrating “Holidays at Filoli” through Sunday, January 7. Take photos with Santa Claus on December 16, 17, 21, 22 and 23 from 10 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. Afterwards, view a dozen festooned Christmas trees inside the estate. Filoli has a designated holiday decor team responsible for installing decorations inside and outside the mansion, and miles upon miles of string lights that drape the interior. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively in the daylight. Daytime admission gains you access to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. Evening admission from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. promises a world of wonder where the garden transforms into a mesmerizing display. With sell-out nights expected, securing preferred dates early is encouraged. Returning favorites like the spectacular 200-foot light tunnel come to life under the stars, while a fresh palette of rich pinks, mystical blues, and warm whites embrace the magic of the night Garden. Every Wednesday at 11am, visitors are welcome to join the Gilded Guide tour led by Filoli’s curators. This exclusive experience unveils the stories that breathe life into the House, revealing the meticulous preparations and behind-the-scenes magic that transform Filoli into a holiday wonderland. The festivities extend into the Woodland Court, open daily from 11 a.m.to 9 p.m. with holiday libations, sweet treats, and warm gatherings by the fire pits. The Quail Café serves seasonal menus with hearty soups, stews, and delightful treats, while the Clock Tower Shop provides a chance to shop locally and discover unique gifts. On January 1, 2024, from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m., the Hair of the Dog Hike also invites participants to rejuvenate and embrace fresh beginnings with this invigorating outdoor experience, plus the infamous “hair of the dog” cure for all post-New Year’s Eve ailments. Last year, the Filoli team installed and decorated 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, over 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceilings create an appropriate adobe for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest of those on display. Filoli Gardens is considered one of the finest remaining country estates of the twentieth century, featuring a 54,000+ squarefoot Georgian revival-style mansion, 16 acres of exquisite English Renaissance gardens, a 6.8-acre Gentleman’s Orchard, and hundreds of acres of Natural Lands with five distinct ecosystems and a 1-mile Estate Trail. The two-story historic Filoli mansion contains 56 rooms, including a large ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debut balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. To purchase tickets and learn more about Holidays at Filoli events, visit filoli.org/events/holidays.

For months, the walkers have been monitoring the construction progress of a garage being built for a Crocker Avenue home owned by Jeremy Bo Droga and his wife, Marie-Elise. The group had talked with Jeremy during the construction, and he had offered the walkers a tour when the project was done. The walkers headed to Wildwood Avenue to Crocker Avenues, where the Drogas’ house is located. Jeremy is a charming Australian and a noted sculptor. According to his website, https:// www.bodroga.com/, his artwork evolves with the type of materials and spaces he encounters. He has exhibited all over Europe, America, and Australia. Marie-Elise is French and Jeremy said there is sometimes a conflict over which flag – the Australian or French – should be on the flagpole in front of their house. The property was named “Strawberry Hills” by the original owners, the granddaughter of Hiram Tubbs who founded the Tubbs Cordage Company and built the famous Tubbs Hotel near Lake Merritt. The house was designed by Albert Farr, and construction was finished in February 1906, two months before the earthquake in San Francisco. The house was Farr’s first major commission in Piedmont. Although it is large, this house suggests an English cottage with rolled eaves on the left front gable. It offers grand views of Oakland, San Francisco, and the Bay. The home withstood the earthquake and must have had a dramatic view of the destruction. The house originally had a garage on what is now the site of the home next door, but that land was sold, and a house was built there in 1957. Jeremy and Marie-Elise bought “Strawberry Hills” in 2020, when they began a threeyear project to create a garage at street level below the raised property of the house. They spent a year and a half working with the Piedmont Planning Commission and three months excavating the hill in front of the house. The Drogas were especially sensitive to respecting Albert Farr’s design in the creation of the garage. They hired Greg Kline, a local architect who incorporated the homeowners’ practical needs with classic, historical design references of Strawberry Hills Estate. The garage is two stories and complements the height of the house. There are columns, arches, and a set of windows on the exterior that echo Farr’s design of the main house. The garage interior is open with 16-foot ceilings that offer light, flexibility, and versatility for future needs. A spiral staircase goes to a rooftop garden and an elevator exists. Landscaping will complete this beautiful project. Jeremy put together a large box of fruits from his pineapple guava trees and invited walkers to take as many as they liked home. In return the group gave Jeremy an appreciative round of applause. After the visit, the walkers headed to Sea View Avenue, and then loop back to the city center. Along the way the Grinch was stealing some Christmas tree lights from a front yard, and Santa and his sleigh were making a visit to another front yard. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: We are heartbroken to announce the passing of our daughter and sister, Lorinda Harris, on November 29, 2023. Shortly before her passing, she was thoughtfully selecting gifts for her nephews in preparation for Thanksgiving. Two weeks later, she was unexpectedly gone as a result of an accident outside her home in Sebec, Maine, leaving the many who loved her devastated. Born on September 21, 1968, she was the daughter of Ted Harris and Karen Oleson, the oldest of five siblings. As a young girl, Lorinda loved the living room dance parties she and her siblings improvised to the tunes of Donna Summer and ABBA. One of her siblings remembers their dad, newly single, taking all five kids up to the family cabin and forgetting to bring sunblock along. After a day at the lake and the sunburns that followed, Lorinda spent the night slathering her four siblings head to toe in Noxzema. She was a concerned helper and a consummate older sister, and whether it was with over-thecounter skin cream or another emblem or demonstration of love, she was always quick to extend herself, especially for her family. This made a real difference when before finishing high school, the family gained three stepsisters from her father’s second marriage to Heidi Clawson. Following a predictable pattern, these new sisters quickly came to look up to and adore her as well. Lorinda was a Piedmont High School Varsity Cheerleader and was often seen driving around town in the family’s wood paneled station wagon, frequently with Lou Gramm blasting on the radio. In a family full of Spanish and Portuguese speakers, Lorinda chose to study German. And while she always insisted that she greatly admired the members of her own family, they couldn’t help but notice that German was the home language of her best friend Michelle Mueller’s family, whose house became a second home to Lorinda during her teenage years. Lorinda was always grateful for the influence of the many loyal friends she enjoyed both in Piedmont and her later homes elsewhere. Upon graduating from high school, Lorinda attended UC Irvine, where she quickly fell in with a wonderful group of friends and sorority sisters in the Tri Delta Sorority. She even went on to serve as the Sorority President. These friendships and relationships brought her immense joy during formative years. articles.text: A turnout of 15 readers gathered at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park on December 4 for the First Mondays Reading Group’s discussion of The Finest Hours by Michael J. Tougias and Casey Sherman. The book was written in 2009 and made into a movie in 2016. Gerry Gragg reported that the action film took some Hollywood license with some departures from fact. The Finest Hours is the true story of two heroic U.S. Coast Guard rescues in the winter of 1952 when New England was battered by the most brutal nor’easter in many years. While the storm raged, two oil tankers, the Pendleton and the Fort Mercer which were built during World War II and not for this kind of sea, both split in two. On shore four young Coast Guardsmen were given what was almost a suicide mission of trying to save the dozens of men huddling inside the broken halves of the two ships. They would have to do it in a 36-foot lifeboat with 70-foot waves crashing around them. It was one of the most daring events in the history of the U.S. Coast Guard. Gerry and Darby Gragg had visited the story’s Coast Guard Motor Lifeboat CG-36500 where it is berthed at Rock Harbor in Orleans, Massachusetts. Gerry also volunteers for the Coast Guard. His and Darby’s experience with the Coast Guard, and their knowledge of sailing, made The Finest Hours especially meaningful. The Coast Guardsmen were simple, modest, young people who had made a commitment of service and were unflinchingly meeting it. The book’s narrative was fast and exciting, and it was a quick, enjoyable read for some of the group. Other readers found the book’s back and forth storytelling between the different ships’ situations didn’t keep them involved. It was sometimes hard to tell which ship was being written about. For others the book seemed like news reporting, and the prose didn’t suit them. This led to the question of how two authors write a book together and produce a common style for it. Other readers said the book didn’t provide an understanding of the main characters, and extraneous people were included who were distractions. Additionally, some readers didn’t get a full sense of the waves and storm’s magnitude, but they did feel the cold the men experienced. The Finest Hours also made clear that different types of books perform different functions. Some make readers appreciate history, others writing styles and word craft, while others are inspirational. Group members said that reading different types of books, fiction for some and non-fiction for others, had made them broader readers, and especially appreciative of The First Mondays Reading Group. The group had previously selected Station Eleven by Canadian writer Emily St. John Mandel for their January read and The Code Breaker by Walter Isaacson for February. A committee led by Lois Price and Laura Goldman had built on Priscilla Wanerus’ book list to develop a new book selection process and candidates file. After Bob Hall presented three of the candidates, Lucky Jim by Kingsley Amis was selected for March. The group’s next discussion will be on January 8th at 1:30 p.m. If the weather is cold or rainy, it will be held inside the Community Hall. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required at https:// bit.ly/3R86PP4. Above is the view of Donner Peak. graffiti covering each wall of the sheds, some pieces more magnificent in detail than other common tag-names. Peeking around unsuspecting corners and behind walls, walkers with keen eyes can find some of California’s most prominent urban artists and large murals that are awe-striking. Proper hiking gear is required at some ice-covered area to prevent slipping and accidental falls. With limited parking at the entrance lot to the tunnels, some may have to park off the road along Donner Pass Road or at the Donner Lake Overlook parking lot. In our five miles of hiking, The Post passed just 27 hikers during our time in the tunnels, but another 13 were huddled around the starting area’s sledding hill toward the China Wall. A second China Wall is inside the long tunnel in the mountainside. Watch for massive ice blocks and icicles during this winter walk. The entire walk has graffiti on the tunnel walls. Some pieces are magnificent and well-detailed, like the mural on the right. To enter this area, hikers can punch in Donner Pass, Summit Haus, or Donner Lake Overlook to their GPS device for common starting areas. Return in the summer to see petroglyphs along McGlashan Point and walk up to Donner Peak. Reprinted from January 2021 Piedmont Post. Piedmont Real Estate Update December 2023 A Year in Review and the Outlook for 2024 To say the 2023 real estate market was a roller coaster is an understatement! The year began with bomb cyclones, bank failures, and tech layoffs. The uncertainty continued with unprecedented interest rate increases and an inventory shortage due to many sellers waiting out the market. Let’s take a moment to reflect on the year behind us and consider the forecast for 2024. Home Retention Reached a Record High New listings have been declining year-overyear for 15 months. * In 2023, homeowners had little motivation to sell. Holding tight to their low interest rates and avoiding capital gains taxes were two top reasons for staying in place, with the added dilemma of where to go next. These concerns resulted in the highest homeownership tenure in decades, with a retention of 12 years. Years Owned Home Before Selling Rent vs. Buy In 2005, David Leonhardt of the New York Times wrote an article entitled “Is It Better to Buy or Rent?” in which he encouraged homeowners to “take another look at renting. ” (We remember when this article came out – yes, we have been around that long!) In our market, if that person sold their one-million dollar home in 2005, they would have missed out on the concerns of the Great Recession. However, they would have also missed out on an average annual appreciation of approximately 6% per year, which compounds and would make that home worth roughly $2.8M today. Recently, Leonhardt published another article entitled “Rent Now, Buy Later, ” and the Economist published a study showing that renting may make sense in many parts of the United States. In 2014, the NY Times developed a fantastic Rent vs. Buy Calculator, which is one of the best we have seen (simply Google NYTimes “Rent vs. Buy Calculator”). Our advice? There can be several reasons, financial and otherwise, that affect a decision about whether now is the right time to buy, sell, or rent. The answer to this question can be very personal and impacted by geography and housing types. If you are contemplating a real estate decision and would like a market expert to help you consider options, feel free to reach out. We would be happy to have a candid conversation and walk you through a personal net sheet. Cost Comparison for a Renter and a Homeowner *Source: California Association of Realtors Buyer Challenges Low inventory presented a double-whammy for first-time homebuyers who were already grappling with far less buying power due to rising interest rates. If you add economic uncertainty resulting from layoffs, difficulty in obtaining insurance, inflation, and unsettling geopolitical events, it’s easy to understand how single-family home sales were down 22.2% *Source: California Association of Realtors The chart above shows a cost comparison for a renter and a homeowner over a seven-year period. The renter starts out paying $800 per month with annual increases of 5%. The homeowner purchases a home for $110,000 and pays a monthly mortgage of $1,000. After six years, the homeowner’s payment is lower than the renter’s monthly payment. With the tax savings of homeownership, the homeowner’s payment is less than the rental payment after three years. Expect rates to remain elevated for the near future, affecting borrowing costs.
